description: Our team of three participated in a hackathon where we collaborated to develop an innovative solution to a real-world problem under a limited timeframe. We combined our skills in programming, design, and problem-solving to brainstorm ideas, develop prototypes, and present our final solution.
summary:
TerraMatch is an interactive research tool that connects Mars site selection with Earth analog testing. We used public NASA and planetary datasets to screen terrain, thermal properties, ice indicators and dust conditions, then selected three Mars regions for closer study. Our explorer presents the evidence and limitations behind each region.

To address the challenge, we investigated Earth sites where specific methods could be tested, including interpreting temperature differences, distinguishing underground radar reflectors and measuring polygon patterns at different image resolutions. Each proposed comparison has a defined purpose and documented evidence gaps.

The project helps researchers decide what to measure next and where Earth experiments could reduce uncertainty before a Mars mission. Our results identify research candidates and testable questions; they do not confirm underground ice or establish validated Earth–Mars matches. Traceable sources and reproducible calculations let others inspect and build on the work.
details:
We developed TerraMatch, an interactive research tool that helps users compare potential shallow-ground-ice research sites on Mars and identify Earth locations where specific investigation methods could be tested. The project combines a map-based explorer with reproducible data processing and evidence records.

Our analysis screened regional Mars data on terrain, thermal properties, water and ice indicators, and atmospheric dust. We selected three regions, MS-01, MS-02 and MS-03, for closer examination. For each region, we checked the original data coverage, measurement scale and limitations. The explorer lets users compare the evidence behind these choices and see which questions remain unresolved.

The Earth comparisons focus on practical tests. Edson Hills in Antarctica offers a possible setting for examining whether temperature differences reflect underground ice or differences in terrain and soil. Bethel, Alaska, provides radar and drilling records for investigating competing explanations for underground reflectors. Cape Blossom, Alaska, provides mapped polygon patterns that help us examine what becomes difficult to measure as image resolution decreases. These comparisons remain research proposals with different levels of validation.

We built the numerical workflow in Python 3.12, using NumPy, pandas, xarray and SciPy for data processing, Rasterio for geospatial work, and Matplotlib for figures. The website uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Cloudflare configured to serve its static assets. GitHub supports version control and collaboration. The Mars workflow ran on an Apple Silicon Mac using CPU computation, without model training or a GPU.

The creative contribution is connecting site selection to a specific question: what should we measure next, and where could we test that measurement against independent evidence? This gives each Earth comparison a clear purpose and makes missing evidence part of the decision.

Our team considered differences in planetary conditions, coordinate systems, spatial resolution, observation dates and data quality. We also checked previous research, tracked shared data dependencies and distinguished measurements from model estimates. The intended impact is to help researchers plan more informative follow-up investigations. Our current results support research priorities and test designs; they do not confirm underground ice, establish validated Earth–Mars matches or identify safe locations for landing or extraction.
